findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words, before anything technical. A newcomer can say what Athena is after the first paragraph.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This URL is Athena's home page, but the title and heading are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer may think they have landed on the wrong site until they read the third paragraph of the intro, which explains that the page is a study.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The intro explains why the page exists: it is a worked example of what Athena can do. That gives the rest of the page a purpose, but almost all of the page after the intro (states, transitions, counters, 44 claims) is about firstmate rather than Athena.
findings.source: A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it

findings.text: The next step is linked near the top, so a newcomer does not have to scroll through the long firstmate study to find out how to start.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: Next steps gives exact commands to clone, install and try Athena, plus the prerequisites. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" ... "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" ... "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The prerequisites do not say which operating systems are supported, or whether a Rust toolchain is needed or installed by setup.sh. That is a fair question, since the intro says Athena is written in Rust.
findings.source: Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code).

findings.text: "Predictions" is not explained anywhere on the page, and the line does not say what the run will change in the user's repository or what it might cost. A cautious newcomer may hold back before pressing Enter.
findings.source: It shows how it read the request and its predictions; press Enter to run it on your repository.

findings.text: This link speaks to the repository owner, but it sits in the intro that every newcomer reads. A first-time visitor has no proposals waiting and could be confused by "your decision".
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to lines at a pinned commit, so the page shows the traceability it promises. A sceptical newcomer can check this for themselves, which supports the intro's claim about accountability.
findings.source: Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end.

findings.text: The firstmate sections are dense and full of jargon, but the terms are defined before they are used and again in the Glossary. A newcomer who wants the detail can follow it; a newcomer who doesn't can skip straight to Next steps.
